nameStory: The 'handsome' in this katydid's name comes from its particularly attractive appearance among the meadow katydids. With its sleek build and elegant proportions, early entomologists thought this species stood out as especially good-looking in the Orchelimum genus. The genus name Orchelimum means 'meadow dancer,' referring to their graceful movements through grasslands.
description: The Handsome Meadow Katydid is a slender, green grasshopper-like insect with long antennae and powerful hind legs built for jumping. These delicate insects are part of the katydid family, known for their musical chirping on summer evenings. They have narrow wings held roof-like over their bodies and thread-thin antennae that can be twice as long as their body. Adults typically measure about an inch long, making them medium-sized among New England's katydids.

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Noticeably slender and elegant build compared to other meadow katydids, with a streamlined appearance that looks almost delicate to the touch

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Extremely long, hair-thin antennae that extend well beyond the body length and feel wispy if gently touched

idTips.label: Wings
idTips.description: Narrow, pale green wings that feel papery and are held tent-like over the back, often with subtle translucent areas

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Overall bright green coloration that may fade to yellowish-green, helping them blend seamlessly with grass stems

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Long, spiny hind legs that feel rough to the touch due to small spines, built for powerful jumping through dense vegetation

habitat: Look for Handsome Meadow Katydids in wet meadows, marsh edges, and tall grass prairies throughout New England's lowlands. They prefer areas with dense, tall grasses and sedges, often near streams, pond margins, or in roadside ditches where the soil stays consistently moist. You'll find them climbing on grass stems and low shrubs, usually staying within a few feet of the ground.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet present; eggs are overwintering in plant stems and soil, invisible to casual observers.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when adults emerge and begin their evening concerts. Listen for their distinctive chirping calls starting in July.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue singing and mating through early fall until the first hard frosts. This is often the easiest time to spot them as vegetation begins to thin.
seasonality.winter: No adults present; the species survives as eggs laid in plant tissues, waiting for spring warmth to hatch.

funFact: Handsome Meadow Katydids can actually 'hear' with their legs! They have tiny ear-like organs called tympana located just below their front 'knees' that detect the songs of potential mates, making their legs function as both transportation and communication devices.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Common Meadow Katydid, but the Handsome Meadow Katydid has a noticeably more slender, refined build. Memory trick: 'Handsome is slim' - if it looks particularly delicate and narrow-bodied among the meadow katydids, it's likely the handsome one.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'katydids,' meadow katydids like this one don't actually say 'katy-did' like their tree-dwelling cousins. Their songs are more continuous buzzes and trills, leading to frequent confusion about which insects are making which sounds on summer evenings.
compareHints: Among its Orchelimum relatives, the Handsome Meadow Katydid is distinguished by its particularly slender build and refined appearance. While the Common Meadow Katydid is more robust and the Black-legged Meadow Katydid has distinctive dark leg markings, the Handsome maintains an overall delicate, streamlined look. The Seaside Meadow Katydid prefers salt marshes, while the Handsome sticks to freshwater wetlands and moist meadows.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Orchelimum relatives, the Lesser Pine Katydid is distinguished by its smaller size and pine habitat association.
